title: Replacing decommissioned renewables will take solar and wind installations to new heights as 2.5 TW of projects reach end of life by the 2040s
gist: Wood Mackenzie's Horizons report says 2.5 TW of global wind and solar will reach end-of-life by the 2040s, making repowering and replacement a major driver of installations: equipment sales are projected to be 60%+ higher in 2050 than 2026 even as net additions slow. Repowering favours prime existing sites but could cut German power prices 12-19% in the 2040s, a hidden risk for post-contract merchant assets.

insights.claim: More than 3.5 TW of global wind and solar capacity is operational, and a further 2.5 TW of projects will face an abandon/life-extend/repower decision by the 2040s.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: End-of-life renewables become a multi-TW replacement market that shapes targets, prices and equipment demand.
insights.locator: More than 3.5 terawatts (TW) of global wind and solar capacity

insights.claim: By end-2026 more than 30 GW of wind capacity will have been decommissioned worldwide, two-thirds of it taken offline between 2022 and 2026, showing wind retirements are accelerating now.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Wind repowering is a present-day market, not a distant one; watch service and repowering order flow.
insights.locator: decommissioning has already begun in the wind industry

insights.claim: Solar started rapid deployment later than wind, but its ageing fleet is set to overtake wind's before 2040.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Solar module replacement demand should ramp through the late 2030s, supporting module makers beyond new-build cycles.
insights.locator: Solar began its rapid deployment later than wind

insights.claim: Repowered projects reach market faster than greenfield ones because they retain existing grid connections, planning approval and community acceptance, bypassing interconnection queues and permitting delays, while capex and opex are broadly similar.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: In queue-constrained markets, existing interconnected sites carry a speed-to-market premium worth pricing into asset valuations.
insights.locator: Repowering offers a compelling economic case

insights.claim: In Germany, wind speeds at sites decommissioned this decade average 4% higher than at new greenfield projects (up to 30% higher), and a 4% wind-speed gain yields roughly 7% higher capacity factors and 7% lower LCOE.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Early-built wind sites occupy the best resource; repowering them beats new builds on cost.
insights.quote: A 4% increase in wind speeds translates into roughly 7% higher capacity factors and 7% lower levelised cost of energy (LCOE), all else being equal.
insights.locator: The quality of established sites makes that advantage significant

insights.claim: A growing number of developers in Europe and the US are acquiring operating projects in prime locations, tearing out the old equipment and building entirely new projects on the same site where land, grid capacity or planning approval is constrained.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Ageing operating assets become M&A targets valued for their site rather than their equipment.
insights.locator: This dynamic is already reshaping how companies approach the market

insights.claim: Governments set renewable capacity targets without accounting for decommissioning, and repowering incentives exist in only a handful of wind markets, pushing owners toward life extension rather than reinvestment.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Expect target shortfalls and possible new repowering subsidies; policy changes would be a catalyst for replacement demand.

insights.claim: The European Commission's 500 GW wind target for 2030 needs about 37 GW of annual additions from 2023-2030, and with 17 GW forecast to be decommissioned in that period, the EU must add an extra 2 GW a year just to offset losses, on top of a build rate it already misses.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The EU 2030 wind target looks further out of reach; watch for policy responses that support European turbine OEM demand.
insights.locator: The European Commission has targeted 500 GW of wind power by 2030

insights.claim: Higher output from repowering existing German sites with new modules and turbines could reduce German power prices by 12-19% in the 2040s.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Long-dated German power price curves may be too high; stress-test merchant valuations.

insights.claim: Projects that roll off long-term contracts onto merchant revenue or corporate PPAs by the 2040s face material downside from repowering-driven price declines, making repowering a key variable in long-term project economics.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Discount post-contract tail value for renewable yieldcos and IPPs in heavily repowered markets.
insights.locator: That is a material downside risk for asset owners

insights.claim: Even as net capacity addition growth slows, global wind and solar equipment sales volume is estimated to be more than 60% higher in 2050 than in 2026 because ageing assets must be replaced at scale.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Counter to a 'peak renewables' narrative, turbine and module OEMs have a long replacement-driven demand tail.
insights.locator: Equipment suppliers prepare for rising demand

insights.claim: In the 2040s, replacements of decommissioned capacity will make up 44% of global wind installations and 23% of solar installations, rising above 70% in some established European markets.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Mature European markets become replacement-dominated; supplier exposure there shifts from growth to renewal cycles.
insights.locator: In the 2040s alone, replacements from decommissioning

insights.claim: Without installations that replace decommissioned projects, global wind and solar deployment would keep falling year-on-year, so renewal changes the sector's long-term growth path.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Growth forecasts that treat renewables as saturating miss the replacement cycle.
insights.quote: Without installations replacing decommissioned projects, global wind and solar deployment would continue to decline year-on-year.
insights.locator: "We are entering a new chapter in the energy transition

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie warns that governments ignoring decommissioning will miss targets, suppliers not planning for replacement demand will be caught short, and owners not factoring repowering into price forecasts risk misjudging their revenue environment.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A checklist for positioning: policy gaps, supplier capacity planning, owner price assumptions.
insights.quote: Suppliers that do not plan for replacement demand will be caught short.
insights.locator: "The full force of this shift arrives in the 2040s
